title: Bank chiefs back AI to electrify their productivity
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn says Australia is facing a more transformative period over the coming five years than in the past century due to AI.
Mr Comyn, addressing the House Standing Committee on Economics in Canberra on Friday, dismissed as “unhelpful” the very negative scenarios around artificial intelligence aired in recent months.
“I think (AI) will deliver significant benefits (to the economy). The only question will be what the time frame will be … I think it’s very important to invest to develop the capability because that gives you strategic optionality,” Mr Comyn said. “You can determine what the time frame is and how to distribute those benefits.” He said the size of CBA’s workforce would probably be smaller in the future due to the technology.
“Our purpose will not change. Strategically, we may make some minor tweaks. There will be areas where there will be productivity opportunities. There will be areas where there will be increasing levels of investment. On a like-for-like basis, I expect there will be fewer roles,” Mr Comyn told the committee.
National Australia Bank boss Andrew Irvine, addressing the committee earlier on Friday, said his bank’s decision last month to axe 2500 roles had nothing to do with AI. Mr Irvine said he believed AI would deliver significant productivity gains across the Australian economy.
“I think this can be one of the big levers for us as an economy to increase supply side productivity and be able, ultimately, for Australia to be able to grow faster than it can today,” Mr Irvine said.
Mr Irvine said for the “vast majority of roles” at NAB, the intent was to use AI to improve productivity, not reduce headcount.
“We’ll be seeking to redeploy people. With bankers, for example, what I would want is for them to meet more customers every week, and so the less administrative work they need to do because AI is helping them, then the more customers they should and could be meeting.” While Mr Comyn said AI would deliver productivity gains and bring about major change across the economy, he pointed to cyber as one of the greatest risks for the bank.
“Cyber is the most challenging non-financial risk and I’ve never seen an acceleration in any risk to match what we’ve seen in calendar year 2026,” Mr Comyn said.
“I am extremely worried about this risk. I think there will be tens of billions of dollars in investment that will be required across the economy.” He identified mid-size companies as at greater risk than smaller operators. While CBA had “tremendous resources” to be able to draw on to assist CBA customers, he warned the demand would be so large the bank “won’t be able to resource it”. “But we are going to do our best and this is an incredibly important risk to try to manage and mitigate,” he said. “It’s not just about the models, it’s not just about vulnerabilities. It’s a network strategy, it’s a containment strategy. You have to basically move to complete automation over time, which is very difficult.”
